Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: People are not what they seem
The world is a dangerous place

issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together' directly conflicts with 'I can talk about what happened very easily.' For a severe mugging-related PTSD profile, markedly fragmented recall and very easy verbal access to the trauma narrative are hard to reconcile as describing the same current memory presentation.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: The Memory node is internally incoherent for a severe mugging/robbery PTSD presentation: 'I can talk about what happened very easily' suggests low avoidance and relatively integrated, verbally accessible trauma memory, whereas simultaneously endorsing very vivid detailed recall and body-based painful reliving implies a highly sensory, distressing, poorly integrated trauma memory. This combination is possible in milder cases, but here it is hard to reconcile clinically within the same Memory profile. The Negative Appraisals items are coherent for robbery trauma, but the Memory selections do not fit cleanly with that node pattern or with the strong Negative Appraisals ↔ Memory linkage in the formulation.

issues.item: Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next
issues.explanation: This item is more characteristic of ongoing threat/safety behavior than of a pure negative appraisal. In this profile, Threat is not endorsed and all Threat-related edges are inactive, while the active formulation is specifically centered on a Memory ↔ Negative Appraisals loop. The mistrust items fit robbery-related appraisals, but 'Constant Vigilance' introduces a prominent current-threat theme that is not supported elsewhere in the profile.

vignette:
Rajan is a 32-year-old South Asian man who works as a housekeeper at a mid-sized hotel in a mid-Atlantic city. He has been married for four years, and until approximately eight months ago, his wife described him as warm, talkative, and reliably optimistic. He presented for an initial intake following a referral from his primary care physician, who had grown concerned about Rajan's deteriorating sleep, social withdrawal, and a series of vague but persistent physical complaints that had no identifiable medical cause.

The incident occurred on an evening in early autumn, when Rajan was walking home from a late shift. Two men approached him from behind in a poorly lit side street, and within seconds one had him pinned against a brick wall while the other drove a knee hard into his ribs and wrenched his arm upward behind his back. They took his wallet and phone. Before they ran, one of them struck him across the lower back with what Rajan believed was a fist or a hard object - he could not be sure, because by then he had squeezed his eyes shut and was simply waiting for it to end. He was left on the pavement, winded, with bruised ribs and a strained shoulder. Physically, he recovered within a few weeks. In every other sense, he has not.

What returned most insistently in the weeks that followed were not images in the conventional sense but sensations: a sudden tightening across his ribs, a hot pressure along his left shoulder, a dull radiating ache in his lower back that arrived without warning and felt entirely indistinguishable from the pain he had experienced against that wall. These episodes could be triggered by almost nothing - shifting a loaded laundry cart at work, reaching overhead to strip a hotel bed, a colleague brushing past him in a narrow service corridor. The pain was real enough that on three occasions he stopped mid-task and had to sit down. His supervisor has noted the interruptions. Rajan has offered no explanation.

He has also found, to his own bewilderment and shame, that he cannot speak about what happened with any coherence. He knows the sequence of events with complete clarity - the footsteps behind him, the wall, the knee, the waiting - but when he attempts to put it into language for his wife or his doctor, something fails. The words dissolve before they reach his mouth. He has tried twice to tell his wife the full story and both times trailed into silence, leaving her more worried than before.

The memories themselves, when they surface, are not vague or dreamlike. They are vivid and precise in a way that Rajan finds deeply unsettling - the grain of the brick against his cheek, the exact pitch of one man's voice, the cold of the pavement through his trousers. The clarity does not feel like remembering. It feels like still being there.

What has changed most visibly, however, is what Rajan now believes about the world and the people in it. He had come to understand the attack not as a random misfortune but as evidence of something he had been naive to ignore: that people are not what they seem, that the friendly faces around him - colleagues, neighbours, even strangers who hold doors - are simply individuals whose intentions he cannot verify. At work, where his role requires him to move through occupied and unoccupied guest rooms, to exchange pleasantries with strangers in hallways, and to accept direction from supervisors he barely knows, this conviction has become a constant, exhausting undercurrent. He is certain that the world is a dangerous place and that he had simply been fortunate not to have understood this sooner. He trusts no one fully now - not the men he works alongside, and, in moments that frightened him most, not entirely his wife either.

It was his wife who ultimately persuaded him to seek help. She told him quietly one evening that she felt she was living with someone she no longer recognised. Rajan came to his first session hoping, above all, to feel less alone inside his own experience - and afraid, most deeply, that what he has become is simply what he now is.
